Points are retained only if they fall within raster cells where the kernel-maximized slope meets the threshold and the original raster cell is valid (not nodata). The output is a cleaned point vector layer containing only qualifying points.

The script generates PDF reports (synthesis, map, and vertices) for cadastral parcels ('logradouro' features) by analyzing spatial overlaps with reference layers (e.g., 'Área Homologada', SHP/WFS/DB layers). It creates memory-based intersection layers (point/line/polygon) filtered per parcel and layer name, computes overlap area/length using CRS-specific geometry calculations, inserts dynamic text (headers, data sources, overlay status), exports atlas-driven layouts (A3 landscape map, A4 portrait synthesis), merges PDFs per parcel, and cleans intermediate layers. Outputs are time-stamped, parcel-named PDFs containing cartographic maps, textual summaries of overlaps, and metadata on data provenance.

The script tests GDAL-based geospatial raster processing algorithms, specifically verifying correct command-line generation for tools like AssignProjection, translate, ClipRasterByExtent, ClipRasterByMask, contour, gdal2tiles, gdalcalc, gdalinfo, gdaltindex, grid interpolation methods (average, inverse distance, linear, nearest neighbor), hillshade, aspect, slope, color-relief, proximity, rasterize, retile, warp, merge, nearblack, rearrange_bands, fillnodata, gdaladdo, sieve, gdal2xyz, polygonize, pansharp, viewshed, and buildvrt. Each test validates the exact GDAL command string (e.g., 'gdaldem hillshade ...') produced by QGIS Processing’s GDAL algorithm wrappers using synthetic test data (e.g., 'dem.tif', 'points.gml', 'polys.gml') located in 'testdata/'. No actual remote sensing analysis, modeling, or export is performed — it is a unit test suite for correctness of GDAL command construction under varying parameter combinations (NODATA, CRS, extent, options, EXTRA flags, etc.). The study area, time range, satellite data, and real-world geographic context are absent; all inputs are local, static, generic test files with no georeferenced meaning beyond internal validation.

The script computes land use change between two categorical raster layers (before and after) using QGIS raster calculator operations. It generates four outputs: (1) a detailed change raster encoding transitions as 'to_category * 10 + from_category', styled with a Viridis-like discrete color ramp; (2) a simplified binary change raster (0=no change, 1=change); (3) a gain raster identifying pixels that transitioned into a user-specified category; and (4) a loss raster identifying pixels that transitioned out of that category. All outputs are automatically applied with custom pseudo-color symbology and added to the QGIS project. The algorithm infers category count from input raster statistics and supports integer-coded land cover classes.

task_name: Export vector layers to RockyFor3D ASCII rasters
task_description: The script exports QGIS vector layers (e.g., rock density, block dimensions, soil type, net parameters) into ASCII raster files compatible with RockyFor3D simulation software. It rasterizes selected vector layers using a reference DEM’s extent, resolution, and CRS; applies predefined GDAL data types per attribute (e.g., 'rocdensity' → GDT_CInt32); writes outputs as .asc files in a user-specified directory; and validates presence of required minimum fields ('rocdensity','rockdensity','d1','d2','d3','blshape','rg70','rg20','rg10','soiltype'). It also supports importing and styling RockyFor3D output rasters (e.g., 'E_95CI.asc', 'Ph_95CI.asc') and creating cross-sectional profiles along vector lines by sampling stacked rasters and exporting CSV for R-based plotting.

The script analyzes output from the Urban Weather Generator (UWG) model to compute and visualize spatial and temporal differences in air temperature between urban grid cells and rural reference data. It reads UWG-generated TARGET output files (e.g., '_UMEP_TARGET.txt'), extracts temperature (column index 11), compares it against rural meteorological data ('_metdata_UMEP.txt'), computes statistics (mean, max, median) per polygon ID, and outputs results either as attribute additions to a vector layer or as GeoTIFF rasters with pseudo-color rendering. Plotting functionality generates time-series graphs of temperature, wind speed, and radiation for selected DOY ranges and grid IDs.

The script models upper plate subduction (UPS) zone node geometries and attributes by generating profile lines from multipoint subduction features, sampling raster depth values, applying sediment thickness corrections, computing subduction geometry using ridge depth and age-dependent parameters, and outputting GeoJSON point features with properties including depth (Z), sediment-corrected depth (Z_WITH_SED), lateral distance (LAT_DIST), setting type (Active_Margin or Z_Subduction), and plate affiliation. Outputs include UPS_profiles_{age}.geojson (profile lines) and UPS_nodes_{age}.geojson (sampled points with physical properties).

The script converts oceanic transform margin (OTM) line features into point nodes representing continent-ocean transitions at specified geological ages. It densifies OTM lines, samples raster bathymetry (from a TIN-derived raster) at midpoints to estimate seafloor depth, applies a paleobathymetric model (PCM) and abyssal sediment accumulation model to compute depth-corrected elevations, and classifies endpoints as 'CONTINENT' or 'OCEAN' based on intersection with continent polygons. Outputs include GeoJSON files: otm_multipoint_{age}.geojson (sampled multipoints), OTM_profiles_{age}.geojson (profile lines), and OTM_nodes_{age}.geojson (classified point nodes with Z, Z_WITH_SED, SIDE, PLATE, and FEAT_AGE attributes).

The script tests QGIS-based spectral library and raster/vector geoprocessing utilities, including spectral profile handling (decodeProfileValueDict), spatial point/extent serialization (SpatialPoint, SpatialExtent), raster array extraction (rasterArray, rasterBlockArray), pixel-geometry conversions (fid2pixelindices, MapGeometryToPixel), band metadata parsing (parseWavelength, parseFWHM), and UI loading validation. It validates correctness via unit tests using synthetic and real hyperspectral datasets (EnMAP, HyMAP, landcover) and verifies interoperability with GDAL, QgsRasterLayer, and QgsVectorLayer APIs.

The script converts selected QGIS vector and raster layers to Speckle objects (VectorLayer or RasterLayer) for interoperability, preserving geometry, attributes, CRS, symbology, and layer structure (including tree hierarchy). It handles extrusion (e.g., polygon-to-mesh), elevation projection, attribute type mapping, renderer conversion (categorized/single symbol), and supports non-geometry tables. Outputs are Speckle-native layer objects with embedded features (Points, Polylines, Meshes, etc.), CRS metadata, field definitions, and renderer definitions — ready for transmission via Speckle. No remote sensing analysis, classification, or time-series processing is performed; all operations are GIS layer serialization/deserialization.

The script extracts shoreline positions from a user-provided raster image (loaded via QGIS as `rasterLayer`) using NIR-band–driven K-means clustering to separate water/non-water, followed by morphological buffering and simplification to derive smooth shoreline vector boundaries. Input is a single local raster file (path obtained via `rasterLayer.source()`), with no explicit satellite or collection filtering — the script operates on pre-loaded imagery in QGIS. The NIR band index is selected interactively (`nir_band = int(dlg.rasterBandASEComboBox.currentText())`), and red/green/blue bands are hardcoded as indices 1,2,0 respectively. Classification uses only NIR values reshaped into a 1D DataFrame; no spectral indices (e.g., NDWI, MNDWI) are computed. Output is a GeoJSON file (`file_name+'.json'`) containing LineString geometries (derived from exterior rings of buffered/simplified polygons), saved to user-specified `output_dir`, and automatically added as a vector layer in QGIS. Time range is hardcoded as '2015-01-01' to '2015-12-31' but is not used in GEE processing (no GEE.ImageCollection loading occurs); it appears only for filename construction. CRS is read from input raster metadata (e.g., EPSG:3857 or 32643/32743 for East Africa), and georeferencing adjustments (`horizontal_step`, `vertical_step`) are applied via numpy array manipulation before writing resampled output. No GEE API calls are present — this is a local raster processing script leveraging `rasterio`, `scikit-learn`, and `shapely`, embedded in a QGIS plugin context.

The script computes terrain-induced radar beam blockage for Chiang Rai radar using real radar geometry (azimuth angles extracted from a reference shapefile of Chiang Rai radar scans), calculates effective beam polygons along each azimuth at range bins (500 m), estimates beam height above sea level using the 4/3 Earth radius model, extracts DEM elevation at polygon centroids, and determines beam blockage status (1=blocked, 0=unblocked) by comparing beam height to terrain height. Outputs include: (1) a memory polygon layer with attributes — elevAngle, radialAng, horizonDis (range in meters), size (beam width in km), heightASL (beam height m ASL), DEM_ASL (terrain height m ASL), BeamBlock (binary); (2) a saved shapefile 'BeamBlockChiangraiRadar.shp'; and (3) a rasterized version 'BeamBlockChiangraiRaster.tif' (500 m resolution, EPSG:32647) where pixel values encode blockage status. Study area is Chiang Rai radar coverage in northern Thailand; time range is not temporal — it is a static geometric/terrain analysis based on fixed radar parameters and a static DEM. Input data sources: radar scan shapefile ('rad_cri_utm201908041300.shp') providing real azimuth angles, and a local DEM GeoTIFF ('DEM_for_CRI_radar.tif'). No satellite or remote sensing imagery is used — all inputs are ground-based radar geometry and topographic data.

The script loads a Digital Surface Model (DSM) raster from a GeoTIFF file into QGIS, validates it, adds it to the project and sets the map canvas extent to match. It then clips the loaded DSM raster to the bounding box of a provided QgsGeometry using GDAL Warp, saving the result to a temporary GeoTIFF file. The clipping handles CRS transformation if the geometry's CRS differs from the DSM layer's CRS. Outputs include the loaded QgsRasterLayer object and the file path to the clipped temporary raster.

The script enables interactive cropping of a local raster image (e.g., scanned map, aerial photo) within QGIS using a rectangle-drawing tool. It computes pixel-accurate crop bounds via GDAL Translate using srcWin parameters derived from the drawn extent and the original layer’s geometry and dimensions. The output is a cropped GeoTIFF file — either saved to the OS temporary directory (default) or user-specified location — and attempts to auto-load it into QGIS’s Georeferencer plugin. If auto-loading fails, the output path is copied to clipboard with instructions for manual loading. No remote sensing data, time-series analysis, classification, or Earth observation metrics are involved; the input is a local, unprojected or poorly georeferenced raster file provided by the user.

task_name: Compute zonal statistics for raster density
task_description: The script computes zonal statistics (e.g., mean, min, max, std, mode) of a raster layer ('DENSIDADE_Albers.tif') over polygon features from a vector layer ('novo.shp'). It reads the raster band, applies scale/offset correction, masks pixel values using rasterized polygons, and writes statistical results (e.g., 'MEDIA' for mean) as new attributes in the input vector layer. The workflow includes bounding box intersection, memory-based rasterization, masked array computation with NumPy/SciPy, and QGIS field updates via PyQGIS data provider.

The script calculates the total area (in km²) where a species is predicted to be present based on a Species Distribution Model (SDM) probability raster. It applies a user-specified threshold to binarize the input raster (values > threshold → 1, else 0), polygonizes the resulting binary raster, filters polygons to retain only those with 'presence' = 1, and computes the summed geometric area using QgsDistanceArea with WGS84 ellipsoid. The output is printed as a single value in km².

The script processes Sentinel-2 satellite imagery (B04 and B08 bands) from a user-provided ZIP file to calculate either the NDVI or MSAVI2 vegetation index. It crops the rasters to a selected field polygon from a PostgreSQL database, performs raster algebra using QgsRasterCalculator, computes zonal statistics over the field area, displays index distribution across five quantile-based intervals with corresponding hectares, plots the index-fertilizer response curve, and generates a polygonized guide shapefile with interpolated fertilizer application values. Outputs include clipped rasters, a classified raster output ('raster_output.tif'), textual index distribution labels, a matplotlib graph, and a final shapefile ('guide_file_*.shp') with 'indexValue' and 'Fertilizin' attributes.

The script computes nine quantitative urban morphological indicators from user-provided geospatial inputs: Building Coverage Ratio (BCR), Compactness Index (CI), Plaque Density (PD), Shape Index (SI), Edge Density (ED), Road Density (RD), Intersection Density (ID), Skyline Index (SLI), and Average Building Height (ABH). Inputs are local files — raster or vector — supplied via QGIS file widgets (e.g., building footprints, height data, road networks, optional analysis boundary). For vector inputs, the script rasterizes them using GDAL with user-specified resolution (default 10 m or 0.0001°), auto-detecting height fields in building vectors. Grid-based analyses (e.g., BCR, CI, PD, ED, ABH, SLI) use a user-defined physical grid size in meters (e.g., 500 m), which is dynamically converted to pixel count based on input raster resolution and coordinate system (geographic vs projected). Road and intersection density analyses accept missing boundaries and offer three fallback strategies: bounding box, convex hull, or buffered road network. Outputs include a GeoTIFF raster of the indicator map, optionally a CSV table with per-grid statistics, and optionally a PNG visualization (only for Shape Index). Styling is applied automatically using a reversed Spectral color ramp. No remote sensing imagery or GEE server-side processing is used — all operations are local (GDAL, OGR, NumPy-based core functions imported from `.core`).

The script computes passive margin cross-sectional profiles and generates point-based node features along them. It reads a preliminary TIN-derived raster (e.g., qgis_tin_raster_prelim_XX.tif), a multipoint layer of passive margin crest candidates (pmc_multipoint_XX.geojson), and continent polygon boundaries. For each multipoint feature, it calculates crest elevation (Z_CREST) and position (X_CREST) using PMConversionTools methods, samples raster depth (Z_RASTER) at the midpoint, computes wedge geometry (X_MAX), and constructs linear profiles via create_profile(). Profiles are clipped to continent polygons, checked for spatial uniqueness, and written as MultiPoint GeoJSON (PMC_profiles_XX.geojson). Finally, it samples points along each profile at 50 km intervals, computes elevation Z using passive_margin_profile_clean(), and exports all points as a FeatureCollection GeoJSON (PMC_nodes_XX.geojson) with attributes including TYPE, FEAT_AGE, DIST, Z, Z_WITH_SED, and PLATE.

The script tiles a digital elevation model (DEM) raster into 512×512 pixel GeoTIFF tiles aligned to the input DEM's coordinate system and pixel geometry, but only saves tiles whose bounding rectangles intersect a reprojected city boundary polygon. It loads the DEM and boundary shapefile using PyQGIS, reprojects the boundary to match the DEM’s CRS if needed, unions all boundary geometries, iterates over regular grid-aligned tile extents, checks intersection with the unioned boundary geometry, and uses gdal_translate with -projwin to extract each valid tile. Outputs are individual GeoTIFF files named 'tile_i_j.tif' saved to a specified output directory.

The script implements a multi-exposure impact analysis framework that concurrently processes ≥2 exposure layers (e.g., population, buildings, roads) with a single hazard layer (e.g., flood, earthquake) and an optional aggregation layer (e.g., administrative boundaries). It orchestrates multiple individual ImpactFunction instances—one per exposure—then synthesizes results into two core output layers: (1) a multi-exposure aggregation summary layer (vector polygon), aggregating impact counts per aggregation unit across all exposures; and (2) a multi-exposure analysis summary layer (vector polygon), representing the union of analysis extents and containing exposure-specific impact statistics. Provenance metadata is rigorously tracked for all inputs (hazard, exposures, aggregation), CRS, analysis extent, datastore URI, and output layers. The workflow includes input validation, CRS/extent consistency checks, layer cloning, parallel IF execution, geometric union of extents, and GIS operations including vector preparation, virtual aggregation creation, and summary statistics computation via safe.gis.vector.summary_5_multi_exposure functions. No satellite imagery, time-series, or pixel-based remote sensing operations are performed—the script operates entirely on preloaded QGIS vector/raster map layers within the InaSAFE desktop or Celery environment. Study area, time range, and sensor/band details are not specified in the code.

task_name: Export vector and raster layers for GeoServer
task_description: The script exports QGIS vector and raster layers into standardized formats (Shapefile for vectors, GeoTIFF for rasters) suitable for GeoServer ingestion. For vector layers not already in Shapefile format, it reprojects and writes them using QgsVectorFileWriter.writeAsVectorFormat with system encoding and original CRS; for non-TIFF rasters, it uses QgsRasterFileWriter to convert via the layer's pipe, extent, CRS, width, and height. Warnings are logged when format conversion is required, indicating potential data loss.

task_name: Validate radar rainfall against gauge rainfall
task_description: The script validates radar-derived rainfall against in-situ rain gauge measurements at 15-minute temporal resolution over the Yom River Basin in Thailand. It reads gauge station coordinates (from '1สถานีวัดฝนกรมอุตุลุ่มน้ำยม2018.csv'), transforms them from WGS84 (EPSG:4326) to UTM zone 47N (EPSG:32647), then spatially extracts radar rainfall values (from GeoTIFF files in 'z_temp/1outp_mosaic_temp/') at each gauge’s UTM location using QgsRasterLayer.dataProvider().sample(). Simultaneously, it reads co-temporal 15-minute gauge rainfall values from CSV files (in '1outp_gauge_temp/1gauge15min/'). For each matched radar–gauge timestamp and station, it pairs the gauge value (column index 2 of the CSV row) and extracted radar value into a tuple. The output is a CSV file ('validate_rr_rg_15min.csv') containing station ID, gauge rainfall (mm), and radar rainfall (mm) — intended for subsequent statistical validation (bias, MSE, RMSE). Study area is explicitly the Yom River Basin; time range is not specified in code but implied by filenames and context as 2018 (from gauge filename '1สถานีวัดฝนกรมอุตุลุ่มน้ำยม2018.csv') and likely aligned with radar mosaic files generated for that year; however, no explicit timestamps or date filtering logic appears in the script — only filename-based matching (e.g., '20200613' in comment is a script version date, not data date). Data sources are local raster (radar mosaics) and tabular (gauge logs); no GEE Earth Engine assets or satellite APIs are used — this is a PyQGIS desktop workflow, not a GEE script despite the prompt's mischaracterization.

The script performs weighted arithmetic aggregation of precomputed raster layers (e.g., factor or dimension outputs) using QgsRasterCalculator. It loads valid rasters from file paths stored in JSONTreeItem attributes, constructs a band-weighted sum expression (e.g., '(w1 * layer_1@1) + (w2 * layer_2@1)'), and writes the result to a GeoTIFF. No new remote sensing data is loaded, processed, or classified; all inputs are pre-generated local rasters (e.g., '*_masked_{index}.tif'). The study area geometry is passed but unused in aggregation logic. Outputs include a single aggregated GeoTIFF per area index and updates to the JSONTreeItem's 'result_file' attribute. Satellite imagery, time series, cloud masking, NDVI, classification, or spectral analysis are not present — this is a post-processing raster algebra step.

The script exports QGIS raster and vector layers to temporary GeoTIFF (.tif) and GeoPackage (.gpkg) files, respectively, using QgsRasterFileWriter and QgsVectorFileWriter. It writes the full extent, resolution, CRS, and data of the input layers to disk in standard geospatial formats. No geospatial analysis, classification, time-series processing, or thematic modeling is performed — the script solely handles I/O conversion and temporary file management for downstream external command execution (e.g., via run_command_stream_output). The study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and thematic analysis methods are not present in the code and cannot be inferred.

The script performs dasymetric downscaling of a user-provided coarse-resolution raster (e.g., VIIRS NTL, LST, or population) to a user-specified target resolution (e.g., 30 m) using Random Forest regression trained on high-resolution covariates (e.g., Sentinel indices, elevation, roads, built-up). It resamples both target and covariates to the target grid using appropriate resampling (bilinear for continuous, nearest-neighbor for categorical), applies spatial-block or random train/test splitting, trains an OOB-enabled Random Forest (200 trees), predicts pixel values across the full extent (optionally in memory-safe chunks), clips predictions to nonnegative values if requested, and outputs (1) the downscaled raster, (2) a CSV with R², RMSE, MAE, OOB score, and feature importances, and (3) a PNG with three panels: observed vs. predicted scatter plot, residual histogram, and horizontal bar chart of covariate importance. No specific study area, time range, or satellite data sources are embedded — all inputs are user-supplied raster layers; the script is generic and agnostic to geography, temporal extent, or sensor origin.

The script generates a topographic map by downloading Copernicus 30m DSM tiles covering a user-defined bounding box (lat_min/lat_max/lon_min/lon_max), mosaicking them into a single DEM GeoTIFF, clipping to the exact extent, computing a hillshade layer, applying a QGIS color ramp to the DEM, overlaying hillshade with transparency, ordering layers (hillshade above DEM), and exporting a high-resolution PNG visualization that combines elevation coloring and shaded relief. The data source is the Copernicus Digital Elevation Model (DEM) hosted on AWS S3; no time dimension is involved as it is a static terrain product. Outputs include: (1) clipped DEM GeoTIFF (_dem.tif), (2) hillshade GeoTIFF (_hillshade.tif), (3) filled DEM GeoTIFF (_Dem_filled.tif), and (4) final PNG topography map (_topography_map.png).

The script classifies two input rasters (Raster A and Raster B) into three quantile-based classes (1/2/3) using tercile breaks (33.33rd and 66.67th percentiles), then combines them arithmetically into a bivariate raster where each pixel value is a two-digit code (11–33) representing the joint class membership (e.g., 11 = low A + low B; 32 = high A + medium B). It optionally reprojects and aligns Raster B to Raster A’s grid, applies a divisor scaling to Raster B, computes tercile thresholds from valid non-NoData pixel values, and outputs three rasters: classified Raster A (1–3), classified Raster B (1–3), and the bivariate composite (11–33).

task_name: Generate ortho and contour graph layers
task_description: The script creates a QGIS project (.qgs file) containing ortho (RGB/IR/IRC), OPI (overlay), surface graph, contour graph (derived via VRT pixel function), and multiple vector layers (patches, remarks, advancement, info save, external vectors). It configures layer visibility by scale, resampling, opacity, CRS, symbology (paletted renderer for contours), and groups layers hierarchically. It also injects macros with dynamic parameters (branch ID, URL, tile matrix set, style, CRS, pixel size) and sets the canvas extent to the ortho layer’s extent.

The script implements a QGIS plugin for calculating land degradation, carbon change, restoration biomass change, and urban change using geospatial workflows. It supports both local execution (via GDAL raster operations like Warp, Clip, Rasterize, Translate) and remote execution (via Trends.Earth API). Key processing steps include preparing area-of-interest geometries, clipping or masking rasters to AOI boundaries, resampling, compressing outputs, and validating output file overwrites. Outputs include georeferenced GeoTIFFs with standardized naming prefixes and suffixes, summary tables, and remote job scheduling.

The script converts a GeoTIFF digital elevation model (DEM) into a Unity-compatible 16-bit little-endian raw binary (.raw) file, applying center-based square cropping (if non-square), zero-padding detection and exclusion in border regions, terrain dimension calculation in meters (X/Z) using geotransform-derived world coordinates, and min-max normalization scaled to uint16 range [0, 65535]. It outputs the .raw file and prints Unity import guidance—including resolution, terrain size (X/Y/Z), elevation range, and projection warnings—based on GDAL dataset metadata and geotransform analysis. Input is assumed pre-reprojected to UTM; geographic inputs trigger warnings but are still processed. No study area, time range, satellite, or external Earth observation data sources are involved—the script operates purely on local raster files provided by the user via QGIS Processing interface.

task_name: Filter raster by identified band values
task_description: The script filters a Sentinel-2 (S2) raster layer in QGIS based on pixel values manually identified via the 'Identify Results' dock widget. It constructs a multi-band logical AND expression using user-interacted band-specific threshold ranges (±900 around each identified value), computes a binary mask using QgsRasterCalculator, saves it as a GeoTIFF, and applies a paletted renderer (transparent for 0, red for 1) to visualize 'Zonas para Scribble'. The input raster is assumed to be a multi-band Sentinel-2 product (e.g., reflectance or index stack), but no preprocessing (cloud masking, scaling, or atmospheric correction) is performed in the script. The output is a binary raster layer named 'Máscara' added to the QGIS project with custom symbology. No study area, time range, or explicit dataset path is defined — the script operates purely on the currently loaded QGIS raster layer(s) whose name starts with 'S2'.

The script retrieves STAC items matching a user-selected date and geometry, extracts red/green/blue band assets from the item's metadata (using 'bdc:bands_quicklook' or fallback bands), constructs VRT rasters via GDAL for RGB compositing, and adds them as valid QGIS raster layers. It relies on pystac_client to query a STAC API, shapely for geometry serialization, and GDAL/QGIS APIs for raster I/O and layer management.

The script computes earthwork volumes (cut, fill, and net) by differencing two DEM rasters (DEM and Base DEM) within a user-provided heap polygon. It rasterizes the polygon to create a binary mask aligned with the DEMs, extracts elevation values only within the masked area, computes the elevation difference array, and sums positive differences (cut volume), absolute negative differences (fill volume), and their net difference. Outputs are three scalar numeric values: cut volume, fill volume, and net volume, reported via QGIS feedback and returned as algorithm outputs.

The script detects agricultural areas and SAP (likely 'Sistemas Agroflorestais' or 'Sistemas de Agricultura de Precisão') from a precomputed COSsim raster dataset ('COSsim_2020_N3_v1_TM06.tif'). It crops the raster to a user-defined UTM-extent (ext = (-57000, -90000, -54000, -89000)), derives binary masks for agriculture (cossim // 100 == 2) and SAP (cossim ∈ {311, 322}), applies circular convolution kernels (e.g., diameter 11, radius 5) to smooth and aggregate these masks, and then combines them using thresholded logical conditions (e.g., fagr > 5/Nref, fsap > 2/Nref, pmin < fsap+fagr ≤ pmax) to produce a final binary map of co-located agricultural–SAP zones. Outputs include two matplotlib visualizations: (1) side-by-side grayscale plots of raw agri/sap masks; (2) four subplots showing convolved+combined results under varying kernel sizes (5×5, 7×7) and iteration depths (7, 9, 11), all rendered with 'viridis' colormap. No GEE server-side export is performed — all processing is local using GDAL, rasterio, NumPy, and matplotlib. The study area is a small UTM-projected region in Portugal (inferred from folder path 'C:\Users\mlc\OneDrive - Universidade de Lisboa\...'), and the input raster is a classified thematic map (not raw satellite imagery), with no satellite, sensor, or band information present in the code.

The script converts the third band (band index 3) of a local PNG raster file (Ljimz.png) into vector polygons using GDAL's Polygonize function. It loads the raster via QgsRasterLayer and GDAL, validates its integrity, selects band 3 explicitly, and writes the resulting polygonized features to an ESRI Shapefile named 'POLYGONIZED_STUFF.shp'. No classification, thresholding, or preprocessing (e.g., reprojection, nodata handling, or band interpretation) is performed — the operation is a direct raster-to-vector conversion of pixel values in band 3. The study area, time range, satellite/sensor, and geospatial context are not specified in the code; the input is a generic local PNG with no embedded georeferencing or metadata evident in the script.

The script performs a raster algebra operation to compute the pixel-wise sum of Band 1 and Band 2 from a single input raster layer (bohLayer) using QGIS's QgsRasterCalculator. It defines two QgsRasterCalculatorEntry objects referencing 'boh@1' and 'boh@2', constructs an expression 'boh@1 + boh@2', and writes the result to a GeoTIFF file at '/home/user/outputfile.tif' using the input layer's extent, width, and height. No classification, masking, or temporal aggregation is performed.

The script performs multi-criteria suitability analysis for school site selection using GIS-based rasterization and proximity modeling. It takes user-provided shapefiles representing criteria (e.g., roads, rivers, existing schools, land use), rasterizes them to a common extent and resolution (28.38985503875978 m) derived from a study area shapefile, then computes Euclidean distance (proximity) rasters for each criterion. The outputs are georeferenced GeoTIFF rasters: (1) binary rasters of input criteria (e.g., 'roads.tif'), and (2) corresponding proximity rasters (e.g., 'prox_roads.tif'). No classification, weighting, or final suitability map synthesis is implemented in the provided code — only preprocessing steps. Study area is defined by an input shapefile; no time-dependent data or satellite imagery is used. All operations are local GDAL/OGR-based, not GEE cloud processing.

The script is a QGIS unit test suite for QgsMapLayerFactory, verifying correct behavior of typeFromString(), typeToString(), and createLayer() methods. It tests string-to-layer-type conversion accuracy (e.g., 'vector' → QgsMapLayerType.VectorLayer), round-trip consistency between typeToString and typeFromString, and successful instantiation of all supported layer types (Vector, Raster, Mesh, Point Cloud, Annotation, Vector Tile) using local test data files (e.g., 'lines.shp', 'landsat.tif', 'lines.2dm', 'ept.json', and synthetic URIs). No geospatial analysis, modeling, or remote sensing operations are performed; outputs are boolean validity assertions, type checks, and name validations within unittest framework.

The script implements a QGIS plugin dialog for submitting geolocated address correction reports to the French Base Adresse Nationale (BAN) API. It enables users to select a point on the map (transformed to WGS84), enter address details, classify the error type (e.g., 'Adresse inexistante', 'Numéro erroné'), provide description and optional correction/email, validate the form, and submit via HTTP POST using an authenticated token. On success, it displays the returned signalement ID and metadata; on failure, it shows error messages. It also supports offline CSV export of the report with timestamp. No remote sensing, satellite imagery, or geospatial analysis is performed — only coordinate capture, form handling, API interaction, and file export. Study area: France (inferred from BAN — Base Adresse Nationale, the official French national address database); time range: not specified; data sources: BAN REST API (no satellite/sensor/bands); outputs: API response confirmation, CSV export file.

The script renders map tiles from a QGIS project file (qgz) at a specified scale using a grid GeoPackage (100k_grid.gpkg) to define tile extents. It sets up QgsMapSettings with NZTM2000 (EPSG:2193) CRS, renders each tile as a PNG using QgsMapRendererCustomPainterJob, then converts the PNG to a georeferenced GeoTIFF via gdal.Translate with TILED=YES, COMPRESS=LZW, and BIGTIFF=YES options. Outputs are scale-tagged PNGs (immediately deleted) and corresponding GeoTIFFs stored in a hierarchical directory structure under 'tiles/qgis-grids/'. The process uses multiprocessing (4 workers) for parallel tile rendering.

task_name: Convert GHSL settlement raster to vector polygons
task_description: The script processes Global Human Settlement Layer (GHSL) raster data to generate vector polygon representations of human settlements. It first reclassifies input rasters (values 10/11 → 0, all others → 1), then cleans rasters by setting 0 values to NoData, polygonizes the cleaned rasters using GDAL's 8-connected polygonization into GeoParquet files, combines multiple polygonized layers optionally filtered by a QgsRectangle extent, and performs spatial joins. All operations use GDAL raw API with no QGIS processing backend; outputs include classified TIFFs, cleaned TIFFs, polygonized GeoParquet files, and combined GeoParquet files.

The script downloads and clips a national high-resolution population raster dataset (Meta HRSL, Italy 2020) to a user-defined area of interest (AOI) using GDAL-based raster clipping. It retrieves the dataset from Humanitarian Data Exchange (HDX) as a GeoTIFF inside a ZIP archive (ita_general_2020_geotiff.zip), extracts the first valid GeoTIFF, reprojects the AOI extent to WGS84 (EPSG:4326), and performs spatial clipping. The output is a clipped GeoTIFF file named 'meta_hrsl_aoi.tif' containing estimated population counts (or density) aligned to the AOI geometry. The study area is implicitly Italy (from filename 'ita_general_2020_geotiff.zip' and resource ID), time is 2020 (from filename), and no classification, modeling, or temporal analysis is performed — only download, extraction, reprojection, and clipping. Satellite/sensor/bands are not applicable: this is a modeled, non-remote-sensing gridded population product.

The script applies a user-defined convolution kernel (e.g., high-pass or Gaussian) to a local GeoTIFF raster file using GDAL's built-in convolution filter via gdal.Translate with the GDAL_CONVOLUTION_FILTER config option. It reads the input raster, applies the kernel (3×3 by default), writes the filtered output to a new GeoTIFF, and reports execution time and success status. The script operates entirely on pre-existing local raster files — no GEE server-side computation, no image collections, no cloud masking, no temporal filtering, and no geographic projection handling beyond what GDAL natively supports. Input/output paths, kernel values, and kernel size are hardcoded or passed as task parameters; no study area, time range, satellite data, or remote sensing metadata is involved. All operations are local CPU-based raster algebra using GDAL’s internal convolution engine.

The script calculates biomass change due to ecological restoration by clipping input biomass difference rasters to an area of interest (AOI), computing spatially weighted summary statistics (initial biomass, biomass change per restoration type, and total site area in hectares), and exporting results to a GeoTIFF and an Excel summary table. It handles AOIs crossing the 180th meridian via WKT splitting, applies nodata masking (-32767), computes cell areas using geodesic latitude-dependent calculations, and aggregates results across tiled raster blocks. Outputs include a clipped/merged biomass difference raster (GeoTIFF or VRT) and a formatted Excel workbook with restoration type-specific biomass metrics.

task_name: Load Azure Maps Creator indoor datasets
task_description: The script loads indoor mapping datasets from Azure Maps Creator API into QGIS as vector layers, organizes them by collection and geometry type (e.g., Point, LineString, Polygon), applies ontology-aware attribute widgets (e.g., ValueRelation for referential integrity), adds floor-aware filtering via level picker, enforces required field constraints, configures labeling and attribute table visibility, and enables synchronized editing (create/update/delete) back to the Azure Maps Features service. It supports two ontologies — Facility 2.0 and Custom — and handles geometryCollection warnings (unsupported in QGIS). Outputs include grouped layer trees, floor-filtered views, read-only attributes, and error-resilient commit workflows with logging and message bar feedback. Data source is Azure Maps REST API (v2023-03-01-preview), not satellite or Earth observation data.

The script generates a YOLOv5-compatible training dataset from QGIS vector and raster layers. It first creates a grid of 1280×1280-pixel polygons aligned to the input raster's ground sampling distance (GSD), then filters out polygons not containing sample points (from 'amostras' layer), clips the raster to each retained polygon, converts clipped GeoTIFFs to JPEGs, and generates corresponding YOLO-formatted label files with normalized bounding boxes centered on sample geometries. Finally, it splits the dataset into train/val subsets (80/20) and organizes files into standard YOLO directory structure (train/images, train/labels, val/images, val/labels).

The script is a comprehensive unit test suite for the QgsVectorLayer class in QGIS, verifying correct behavior of vector layer operations including feature creation, editing (add/delete/change features/attributes/geometries), field management (add/delete/rename/alias/constraint/expression fields), joins, selection, aggregation, rendering, metadata handling, and layer cloning. It uses memory-based layers and test datasets from QGIS test data paths (e.g., 'points.shp', 'lines.shp', 'bug5598.shp', 'joins.qgs') to validate correctness through assertions. No geospatial analysis or modeling is performed; outputs are test pass/fail results.

The script identifies invalid geometric intersections between contour lines and drainage (stream) lines in a GIS environment using QGIS Processing algorithms. It performs spatial join between the two line layers, computes intersections, and flags cases where intersections are non-point geometries (e.g., lines or multi-lines), indicating topographic inconsistencies such as streams crossing contours without proper elevation logic. Outputs include point flags (for multi-point intersections) and line flags (for line/multi-line intersections), both derived from the input stream layer’s geometry and fields.

The script analyzes HEC-RAS 2D hydraulic model output stored in HDF5 format to distinguish fluvial (river-driven) from pluvial (rainfall-driven) flooding based on flood arrival timing. It reads mesh cell centers and maximum water surface times, classifies cells using a user-defined time threshold (delta_t in hours), computes shared edges between adjacent cells, identifies boundary lines where flood arrival time difference exceeds delta_t, and optionally outputs either boundary line features or classified polygon areas (fluvial/pluvial). Outputs include QGIS vector layers: LineString boundaries or Polygon areas with attributes including area measurements and type labels.

The script generalizes line and multiline features in a QGIS vector layer using the Douglas-Peucker algorithm (via QgsGeometry.simplify()). It reduces vertex count while preserving overall shape, supporting two output modes: (1) in-place modification of the original layer (with optional auto-commit and edit-mode handling), or (2) creation of a new memory-based (or optionally permanent) generalized copy layer. Input parameters include tolerance (distance threshold in map units), selection filtering (all vs. selected features), and storage options. Outputs include updated geometry, vertex reduction statistics, success/warning messages with quantitative summaries (e.g., 'Total vertices: 12456 → 3892 (reduced by 8564, 68.8%)'), and history records for undo/redo via stored WKB geometry payloads.

The script creates distribution maps for taxa based on point localities and a polygon grid layer. It selects localities by taxon attribute, intersects them with grid cells using spatial indexing, generates a memory vector layer of selected grid cells, applies styling from the grid layer, and renders map images (PNG) for each unique taxon. Inputs include base, secondary, surface, localities, and grid layers; outputs are PNG maps named after each taxon in a user-specified output directory.

The script calculates the Nearest Neighbor Index (NNI) for point features within each polygon feature. It computes observed mean distance, expected mean distance, NNI ratio, standard error, and z-score per polygon. Input requires a polygon layer and a point layer; output is a polygon layer with added fields: point_cnt, area, obsavgdist, expavgdist, nni, zscore, and stderr. The algorithm uses Euclidean distance between points and applies standard spatial statistics formulas for clustered/random/dispersed pattern assessment.

task_name: Calculate urban environmental and social indexes
task_description: The script calculates three categories of urban indicators: (1) permeability indicators (RIE, BAF, and Indice di Permeabilità) per cadastral lots (ID_Lotto), derived from material-specific coefficients applied to surface, vegetation, building, and tree layers; (2) green urban indicators (Verde Urbano Fruibile per capita and number of public trees per 100 residents) aggregated by basin ID (ID_Bacino); and (3) social indicators (parking area per capita, number of family units, persons per housing unit, covered public space per capita, open public space per capita) also aggregated by basin ID. Outputs are new QGIS vector layers with graduated symbology: 'Indicatori_RIE', 'Indicatori_BAF', 'Indicatori_IPerm' (polygon layers per lotto), 'Indicatori del Verde Urbano' (polygon layer per bacino), and 'Indicatori Sociali' (polygon layer per bacino). All calculations respect user-defined filters for basin IDs, property type (public/private), and layer/attribute selections. No satellite or remote sensing data is used — all inputs are local vector layers loaded from the QGIS project.

The script calculates interior angles at each vertex of a selected polygon feature (single or multipart) using vector geometry. It extracts ordered vertices, computes the angle between consecutive edge vectors via dot and cross products, handles closed-ring topology with proper index wrapping, and outputs a point layer where each feature represents a vertex and stores the computed angle (in degrees or radians). Optional visual arc geometries are generated to illustrate angles. The output layer includes configurable fields (angle value, vertex index, source feature ID) and automatic labeling showing angle values with unit symbols.

The script creates a 100 km buffer polygon (circle) centered on Fort Nelson, British Columbia, using geocoded coordinates from the Nominatim API. It reprojects the point from WGS84 (EPSG:4326) to UTM zone 30N (EPSG:32630), generates a circular buffer with 64 segments, and exports the resulting polygon as a shapefile ('circle_100km.shp'). The layer is added to the current QGIS project. No time-based filtering or remote sensing data is used.

The script computes the centroid geometry for each feature in an input vector layer that satisfies a user-defined QGIS expression filter. It reads a vector layer with any geometry type, applies a filter expression via QgsFeatureRequest, calculates the centroid of each matching feature's geometry, preserves original attributes, and outputs a new point layer containing only those centroids. The algorithm also returns the count of filtered features. It is implemented as a QGIS Processing Algorithm named 'Filtered Centroids' under the 'Example scripts' group.

task_name: Clip imagery and DEM to AOI
task_description: The script extracts and exports georeferenced imagery and DEM data clipped to a user-defined vector-based Area of Interest (AOI) in QGIS. It renders visible map layers at a specified CRS and resolution, applies a vector-derived mask to the rendered image, auto-crops the masked image to its opaque bounds, and clips a DEM layer to the corresponding geographic extent using GDAL warp with reprojection and optional resolution matching. Outputs include a cropped PNG texture image (TIFF_Textures/Tile__0__0.png) and a georeferenced GeoTIFF DEM file (e.g., output_name.tif), both aligned to the AOI’s geometry and coordinate system.

The script detects surface water using Sentinel-1 GRDH imagery (IW mode, VV polarization) processed through calibration, subset to AOI intersection, terrain correction, speckle filtering (NLM), and Otsu thresholding. It outputs binary water masks (8-bit GeoTIFFs) clipped to the input AOI shapefile, with optional temporal stacking for multi-temporal minimum backscatter analysis. Outputs are saved in a subdirectory 'step6_sar_watermasks' under the specified output directory.

The script eliminates sliver polygons from a selected set of features in a QGIS vector layer by merging them with adjacent polygons based on either shared boundary length (if 'boundary' option is checked) or largest intersecting area. It iterates over selected feature IDs, computes geometry intersections, identifies optimal merge candidates, combines geometries, and writes the result to a new shapefile or updates an existing layer. Outputs include a modified vector layer with slivers merged or removed, and optional canvas addition.

The script converts a QgsRasterLayer into a vector layer (shapefile) by raster-to-vector polygonization using GDAL's Polygonize function. It reads the raster source via GDAL, preserves spatial reference, creates a shapefile with one integer field (either 'exposure_type' or 'hazard_value', truncated to first 10 chars), polygons all non-NoData raster values, then deletes features where that field equals the global no_data_value. The output is a QgsVectorLayer with updated keywords including layer_geometry='polygon' and inasafe_fields mapping the output field. No study area, time range, satellite data, or specific geographic extent is referenced—the input is generic QgsRasterLayer with no embedded temporal/spatial metadata in the code; all I/O is abstracted through QGIS layer objects and InaSAFE keyword system.

The script validates whether features in feature_class_2 lie within a specified distance (in meters) of any feature in feature_class_1. It creates a non-dissolved buffer around feature_class_1, builds a spatial index on the buffer geometries, and for each feature in feature_class_2 checks intersection with buffered geometries. Features from feature_class_2 that do not intersect any buffer are reported as validation failures with messages including objectid and country attribute. The output is a list of ValidationResult objects containing those non-proximate features.

task_name: Rank points by value within grid cells
task_description: The script assigns a rank to each point based on its numeric value relative to other points within the same grid cell (polygon), using either maximum or minimum value ordering. It first identifies which grid polygon contains each input point, then sorts points per grid ID by the specified numeric field (ascending for 'Min', descending for 'Max'), and assigns sequential ranks starting from 1 within each grid. Points outside all grids receive grid ID -1 and rank 0. Outputs include the original point layer with two new numeric fields: one storing the containing grid’s ID and another storing the rank.

The script performs a vector geometry dissolve operation on polygon or line input layers in QGIS Processing framework. It either merges all features into a single geometry (when 'Dissolve all' is enabled) or groups features by specified attribute fields and unions geometries within each group using QgsGeometry.unaryUnion() (for grouped dissolve) or QgsGeometry.combine() (for global dissolve). Input validation includes checking for empty geometries and running QgsGeometry.validateGeometry(); errors are logged but not fatal. The output is a new vector layer with dissolved geometries and attributes preserved from the first feature in each group (for field-based dissolve) or from the first input feature (for global dissolve). No remote sensing data, time series, satellite imagery, classification, or raster operations are involved — it is purely a desktop GIS vector processing algorithm implemented in QGIS Python Processing API. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and geospatial analysis methods beyond geometric union are not specified.

task_name: Blur point layer for privacy protection
task_description: The script applies spatial blurring to a point vector layer in QGIS using a configurable radius (in map units), optionally constrained by an envelope polygon layer. It supports exporting the blur radius and centroid coordinates as new attributes. The output is a new polygon vector layer where each input point is replaced by a buffered polygon or clipped to the envelope, generated via the Blur class and written using QgsVectorFileWriter.

The script creates individual 5-unit buffers around each feature in the currently active QGIS vector layer using QgsFeature.geometry().buffer() with 2 segments per quarter circle. It iterates over all features via the data provider's feature iterator and updates geometries in-place without saving to a new file. The commented-out section shows an alternative approach using QgsGeometryAnalyzer().buffer() to write separate shapefiles for the first 5 features with 5000-unit buffers.

task_name: Geocode CSV addresses to ETRS89 coordinates
task_description: The script geocodes a CSV file containing address components (e.g., street name, number, district/barrio) by matching them against internal geographic zones (barri/districte) and assigns ETRS89 X/Y coordinates. It supports fallback extrapolation using centroid points of administrative zones (barri or districte) when direct geocoding fails. Outputs include a modified CSV with appended 'QVISTA_ETRS89_COORD_X', 'QVISTA_ETRS89_COORD_Y', and 'INFERIT_DE_ZONA' fields, saved either to a user-specified path or a default '_out.csv' location.

The script reprojects an input vector layer to the French national coordinate reference system EPSG:2154 (RGF93 / Lambert-93) and saves the result as a new Shapefile with '_2154' appended to the filename in the same directory as the input. It uses QGIS Processing's 'native:reprojectlayer' algorithm, then writes the reprojected layer using QgsVectorFileWriter.writeAsVectorFormatV2 with UTF-8 encoding and ESRI Shapefile driver.

task_name: Manage QGIS job deletion and layer cleanup
task_description: The script provides utility functions for a QGIS plugin to manage geospatial job lifecycle operations, including deleting jobs with user confirmation, removing associated layers from the QGIS project, generating VRTs for specific bands, opening QGIS projects externally, and handling file paths, icons, and logos. Key workflows include confirming job deletion via QMessageBox, iterating over job results to remove matching layers by source path, building single-band VRTs using GDAL, and locating QGIS binaries and processing tools across platforms.

The script computes spatial adjacency (touching or intersecting) between polygons in a shapefile (dyadcells.shp) using QGIS Python API. It builds a spatial index for efficient bounding box intersection queries, then tests non-disjoint geometry relationships to identify neighbor pairs. The output is a CSV file (dyadpolyneighbors.csv) listing each polygon's identifier (cid) paired with each of its neighboring polygon identifiers (ncid), one row per neighbor relationship.

task_name: Calculate scene density with coordinate fixes
task_description: The script calculates spatial density of satellite scene footprints (e.g., PlanetScope) over a user-defined region of interest (ROI), using rasterization as the default method. It implements critical coordinate system corrections—including proper north-to-south raster transform orientation, ROI geometry validation and fixing (e.g., `poly.buffer(0)`), and explicit handling of geographic alignment to eliminate mirrored/flipped outputs. Inputs are scene geometries (as GeoJSON Polygon/MultiPolygon) and an ROI geometry; outputs include a GeoTIFF raster where pixel values represent scene count per grid cell, comprehensive statistics (mean/max/min density, coverage %, histogram), and an enhanced QML style file for QGIS visualization. The script includes robust PROJ/CRS fallbacks during export, chunked processing for large ROIs, and supports full-grid (unclipped) or ROI-clipped analysis modes. No specific satellite imagery pixels or spectral bands are processed—only vector footprints. Study area and time range are not embedded in the core logic; they are fully user-provided via `scene_footprints` and `roi_geometry`.

task_name: Generate weather scenarios for fire simulation
task_description: The script generates hourly weather scenario files (Weather.csv or WeatherN.csv) for the Cell2Fire-W wildfire simulator using Chilean meteorological station data from Valparaíso to Araucanía (32°S–40°S). It selects the three nearest stations to a user-provided ignition point, filters days where daily maximum temperature exceeds a specified quantile (e.g., 0.75), samples consecutive hours starting from a user-defined time, and outputs CSV files containing Scenario, datetime, WS (wind speed), WD (wind direction), TMP (temperature), and RH (relative humidity). Wind direction is flipped (180° offset) before writing. Output files are written to a user-specified directory.

The script selects features from the active QGIS vector layer where the 'aantal_inwoners' (number of inhabitants) attribute exceeds 200,000, then exports only those selected features to a GeoJSON file named 'inwoners.geojson'. It uses QgsExpression to filter features, collects their IDs via QgsFeatureRequest, applies selection on the layer, and writes the selected features using QgsVectorFileWriter with 'onlySelected=True'.

The script computes general and descriptive statistics for vector or raster layers in QGIS, including total count, null count, mean, standard deviation, variance, skewness, min, max, median, and quartiles (25%, 75%). It dynamically adapts to layer type (vector/raster), selects appropriate fields or bands, applies user-specified decimal precision, and populates a UI form with results. Outputs are displayed in QLineEdit widgets (e.g., mean, std dev, quantiles) and not exported as files or layers.

The script tests QGIS Processing algorithms that download OpenStreetMap (OSM) data via the Overpass API for specific geographic queries (raw, spatial area, 'in', 'around', and extent-based), returning vector layers split by geometry type (points, lines, multiline strings, multipolygons) representing OSM elements matching the query criteria (e.g., amenity=bench). Each test mocks HTTP responses to validate correct algorithm behavior, input parameter handling (e.g., timeout, server URL, CRS-aware extent reprojection), and output layer instantiation.

task_name: Count vehicle trajectories at traffic gates
task_description: The script tests the 'export_to_json' algorithm of the Traffic Trajectory Toolkit (TTT) in QGIS Processing. It first runs 'count_trajectories_gate' to compute per-gate traffic metrics (vehicle count, average speed, average acceleration) from point-based trajectory data and line-based gate geometries, then exports the resulting gate-layer attributes—including channel, traveler class, time interval bounds, vehicle_count, speed_avg, acceleration_avg—into a JSON array with one object per gate. The test validates that exactly 3 gates are exported, each with 7 specific fields and correct keys.

The script tests the behavior of a QGIS plugin ('AppendFeaturesToLayer') when updating spatial target layers using non-spatial source layers (e.g., database tables without geometry). It verifies that attribute updates occur correctly for matching features (by key field 'name'), appended features receive NULL geometries, and existing geometries in the target layer remain completely unchanged — confirming geometry preservation during attribute-only updates.

The script performs spatial arithmetic operations (difference, sum, maximum) on user-selected GIS vector layers representing atmospheric deposition (e.g., NH3, NOX), validating input layers for mandatory fields ('fid', 'dep_NH3', 'dep_NOX'). It executes QGIS Processing algorithms ('imaer:relate_difference', 'imaer:relate_sum', 'imaer:relate_maximum') to generate a new output vector layer with computed deposition values, applies IMAER-specific styling, and adds the result to the QGIS project. The workflow is interactive via a dialog with configurable layer inputs and operation type selection.

The script performs hybrid image segmentation (using slope computation, averaging multi-band inputs, watershed segmentation, and vectorization) on user-provided raster inputs, then conducts three-tiered evaluation: (1) Generalization assessment (over/under-segmentation) by counting intersecting polygons between segmented output and up to three reference vector layers; (2) Geometric evaluation comparing area and perimeter of matched reference–segment pairs, generating R² scatter plots and bar charts; (3) Spatial correctness evaluation via buffered clipping of reference polygons, raster clipping, and pixel-level accuracy calculation (boundary vs. region pixel ratios) across user-defined buffer widths — all outputs written to an organized folder with Excel reports, PNG visualizations, and text summaries.

task_name: Calculate terrain suitability for villa placement
task_description: The script calculates a weighted, multi-criteria terrain suitability score (0–100) for residential villa placement on Koh Phangan, Thailand. It computes four component rasters — slope suitability (based on degree thresholds: 0–15°=100, >35°=0), view orientation suitability (based on aspect direction with preferential scoring for south/southwest for sea/sunset views), access distance suitability (distance from roads or parcel centroid, scored 100 at 0–20 m down to 10 beyond 100 m), and drainage safety suitability (using flow accumulation statistics or inverse slope as proxy). These are combined using fixed or configurable weights (40% slope, 20% each for view, access, drainage) into a final suitability raster. Outputs include five georeferenced GeoTIFFs: slope_suitability.tif, view_suitability.tif, access_suitability.tif, drainage_suitability.tif, and suitability_combined.tif — plus statistical validation (mean, histogram by class, validation checks) and human-readable interpretation of site quality (e.g., 'Excellent overall site quality' if mean ≥ 80).

The script processes the AW3D30 30m global DEM to create a standardized, reproducible Koh Phangan Terrain Base dataset in EPSG:32647 (UTM Zone 47N), including multi-angle hillshades, slope (raw and classified), aspect, 10m contours, hydrologically conditioned flow direction and accumulation, stream network (raster and vector), watershed delineation (if pour point provided), and client-specific clipped derivatives — all structured into a hierarchical folder system with LandWise-compliant styling and validation.

The script computes a Canopy Height Model (CHM) by subtracting Digital Terrain Model (DTM) rasters from Digital Surface Model (DSM) rasters, sourced from LIDAR-derived tile datasets referenced in a vector layer ('tile_dsm_dtm.gpkg'). It supports optional post-processing: removal of negative values (ground-level or below), application of a maximum height threshold, resampling to user-defined resolution (with lat/lon-aware conversion), reprojection to target CRS, and clipping to an AOI polygon layer. Outputs include individual CHM rasters per tile (in user-specified format, e.g., GeoTIFF), a merged/clip raster, and a new vector layer documenting processed tiles with updated P_CHM/N_CHM/EPSG_CHM attributes.

The script performs multi-criteria land suitability analysis for landfill site selection by integrating and processing spatial constraints and suitability factors. It begins with vector-based exclusion (e.g., faults, drainages, roads, airports, protected areas, settlements, surface water, rivers) via buffering and sequential difference operations to derive a constrained study area ('Difference.shp'). Then it rasterizes and processes 14 thematic layers — including proximity rasters (8), land use, permeability, water level, elevation (DEM), aspect, slope — all masked to the constrained extent. Each raster is reclassified using user-defined thresholds (via table widget) into suitability scores (e.g., 1–5), and finally weighted linearly using user-specified weights (14 weight fields) via raster calculator to produce a final weighted sum raster ('SumOfWeight.tiff') representing relative landfill suitability across the study area.

task_name: Model wildfire ignition risk using climate and fuel data
task_description: The script generates a spatiotemporally resolved, point-based wildfire ignition dataset for British Columbia (2000–2024) by integrating satellite-derived fire hotspots (filtered by date and clipped to BC), randomly sampled non-fire control points (stratified within BC boundary), and co-located biophysical variables: six climate variables (u10_wind, v10_wind, dew_temp_2m, temp_2m, tot_precip, lai_high) from GRIB-based climate rasters and Fuel_Type from the National FBP Fueltypes raster. It outputs cleaned, merged, and climate/fuel-sampled CSV files per month/year — each containing latitude, longitude, month, year, fire label (1/0), and all environmental covariates — culminating in a single combined CSV for machine learning modeling of ignition probability.

The script processes LiDAR-derived Digital Terrain Model (DTM) and Digital Surface Model (DSM) rasters to compute a normalized height (Canopy Height Model, CHM) raster by subtracting DTM from DSM. It then applies a height threshold (>1.2 m), masks out built-up areas using buffered Ordnance Survey MasterMap boundaries, and vectorizes the resulting CHM to generate candidate tree polygons. These are filtered by minimum area (≥10 m²), then refined using SAGA-based watershed basins on an inverted CHM to identify individual tree crowns. Final outputs include: (1) a shapefile of matched, height-validated, property-buffered tree polygons ('_trees_matched_filtered.shp'), where each polygon is associated with maximum height (_max) and intersected property identifiers; and (2) auxiliary files including clipped CHM, basin polygons, zonal statistics, and cleaned buffers.

task_name: Extract and process climate raster bands
task_description: The script extracts time- and month-specific climate variable bands (e.g., temperature, precipitation) from GRIB-formatted climate model output files (e.g., '2000-2001.grib'), filters them by year/month using GRIB_VALID_TIME metadata and adjustment logic for cumulative variables, clips the resulting rasters to British Columbia’s boundary, reprojects them to EPSG:3347 (NAD83 / BC Albers), fills NoData pixels per band using GDAL's fillnodata algorithm, stacks the filled bands into a multi-band GeoTIFF, and loads the final product into QGIS as a layered raster — all for each month from 2000 to 2024.

The script extracts a binary surface water mask from a pre-downloaded satellite image raster by thresholding the blue band (band 3) between DN values 75–100. It applies NoData masking, gap-filling via interpolation, re-binarization (≥0.5 → 1), sieving to remove small noisy regions (<500 pixels), and polygonization—retaining only polygons with DN=1 to guarantee water-only vector output. Final outputs include a cleaned 0/1 raster mask and a GeoPackage of water body polygons.

The script identifies contiguous raster cells with population ≥300 per cell, groups them into spatially connected clusters (using GRASS r.clump), filters clusters whose total population sum ≥5000, clips and smooths the resulting cluster raster using a majority filter (5-of-8 neighborhood rule) to fill nodata gaps and reduce noise, then converts the smoothed cluster raster into vector polygons. The final output is a shapefile (HighDensityClusters.shp) where each polygon represents a statistically and spatially coherent high-density urban cluster derived from gridded population data.

task_name: Generate topographic surface from contour lines
task_description: The script converts a vector layer of contour lines ('Horizontals.shp') into a raster digital elevation model (DEM) via TIN interpolation; computes its basic statistics (min/mean/max); adds a constant offset (+4842) to the DEM; then derives aspect and slope rasters, followed by reclassification of slope into five ordinal classes (0–10°→1, ..., 41–50°→5). Outputs include: Horizontals_Tin.tif (interpolated DEM), Horizontals_Tin_Calc.tif (offset DEM), ASP.tif (aspect), SLP.tif (slope), and Rec_SLP.tif (reclassified slope).

task_name: Download and mosaic OPR DEM tiles
task_description: The script downloads USGS 3DEP Original Project Raster (OPR) Digital Elevation Model (DEM) tiles that spatially intersect a user-provided Area of Interest (AOI) polygon, filters them by ground sample distance (GSD) to prioritize highest-resolution tiles, creates a seamless GDAL-based mosaic (VRT + warp), optionally clips the mosaic to the AOI bounds, converts elevation values from meters to feet, and optionally generates contour lines at a specified interval in DXF, Shapefile, or GeoPackage format — all saved to a user-specified output folder with a manifest CSV listing downloaded tiles and metadata.

task_name: Generate SWAT HRUs from landuse soil slope rasters
task_description: The script generates Hydrologic Response Units (HRUs) for the SWAT hydrological model by spatially intersecting and aggregating landuse, soil, and slope raster grids with watershed subbasin and channel delineation data. It supports multiple HRU generation strategies (dominant HRU, dominant landuse/soil/slope, or threshold-based filtering by area/percentage of landuse, soil, or slope classes), incorporates landscape units (floodplain/upslope), handles reservoir/pond identification and merging, produces shapefiles (FullHRUs, actual HRUs, LSUs), writes HRU metadata to a SQLite database (gis_hrus, gis_subbasins, gis_lsus, gis_water), and generates comprehensive text reports (topographic, basin, HRU).

The script performs plate-by-plate TIN interpolation of elevation-like node points (water-load-corrected) in a global equal-area projection (ESRI:54034), followed by nodata filling and polygon clipping per tectonic plate, ultimately generating a mosaic of plate-clipped rasters to produce a final filled global elevation raster for a given geological age. Inputs include precomputed point layers ('all_nodes_*.geojson') tagged with plate names (e.g., 'Nazca', 'India') and appearance age, and plate polygon layers ('Plate Polygons') filtered by age. The workflow includes longitude clamping, reprojection using CEA (Cylindrical Equal Area), buffering to refine plate boundaries, spatial filtering of nodes by plate identity and intersection, per-plate interpolation, clipping to refined plate polygons, and mosaicking.

task_name: Simplify flight waypoints using DEM-constrained 3D tolerance
task_description: The script simplifies a drone flight plan (input CSV with longitude, latitude, and altitude(m)) by: (1) converting points to a 3D vector layer in WGS84; (2) sampling elevation values from a user-provided DEM raster; (3) reprojecting to a user-specified projected CRS; (4) constructing the original trajectory line ordered by 'original_index'; (5) simplifying that line using Douglas-Peucker (tolerance parameter); (6) extracting vertices of the simplified line; (7) buffering those vertices; (8) spatially joining original reprojected points to buffers to identify which original waypoints fall within tolerance envelopes; and (9) filtering the input CSV to retain only those rows whose line index matches the retained waypoints — producing a reduced, terrain-aware, Litchi-compatible CSV output. Optional outputs include original CSV points, simplified trajectory line (with arrow styling), and simplified CSV points layers added to QGIS project.

The script processes precomputed dNBR raster files (downloaded from Google Earth Engine and stored in the user's local directory) to extract burned areas by reclassifying dNBR values into binary burn/no-burn classes, converting rasters to vector polygons, removing non-burn pixels, dissolving adjacent burn polygons, computing burned area in square kilometers, assigning a cluster-specific identifier, and merging all per-cluster burned area shapefiles into a single national/regional atlas shapefile (BurnedAreaAtlas.shp) with attributes including ClusterId and Area(sqkm).

The script processes high-resolution eReefs hydrodynamic model grid shapefiles to derive simplified, buffered boundary polygons for spatial containment checks. It first dissolves grid cells where depth > 0 to extract the model domain boundary, then applies a buffer (in degrees) followed by geometry simplification (tolerance = 2 × buffer distance) to create a low-detail version suitable for fast point-in-polygon queries—intentionally over-inclusive to avoid false negatives during inverse distance weighted interpolation of model outputs. Outputs include: (1) dissolved high-res boundary shapefiles (.shp and .geojson), (2) buffered intermediate shapefiles, and (3) simplified low-detail boundaries in GeoJSON format with filenames suffixed '_ld-boundary.geojson'.

The script builds a cartographic elevation diagram for Brazilian Army topographic mapping. It processes elevation point data (elemnat_ponto_cotado_p), generalizes them based on map scale, generates terrain slicing rasters (elevation classes) and contour layers from a digital elevation model (MDE), integrates hydrography (cobter_massa_dagua_a, elemnat_trecho_drenagem_l), infrastructure (infra_vala_l), and area-without-data masks (llp_area_sem_dados_a), applies QGIS layer styles from local QML files, configures layout grids with custom annotation expressions aligned to SIRGAS/4674 CRS, inserts SVG-based color bars scaled to class count (2–4 classes), and optionally generalizes drainage networks using geometric constraints. Outputs include styled raster/vector layers added to the QGIS project, updated print layout items (map extent, grids, scale bar, class labels), and a grouped layer tree node for visualization control.

The script computes the closest point on a line feature to each input point, returning a table with five columns: input_id, input_lat, input_lon, line_lat, line_lon. It achieves this through a multi-step workflow: (1) fixing geometries and converting multipart to singlepart; (2) adding XY coordinates to points; (3) using GRASS v.distance to generate shortest-distance line segments; (4) joining attributes and extracting vertices from those segments; (5) filtering for the vertex on the target line (using 'distance > 0' condition); and (6) copying and renaming coordinate fields to produce the final output with standardized field names. The method find_closest_coordinates_from_points_to_lines encapsulates this entire workflow and returns a vector layer with the computed coordinates.

The script extracts sub-watersheds from a segmented stream network (CRHQ) using D8 flow direction rasters, assigns segment IDs to each sub-watershed polygon, computes total watershed area, reclassifies MELCCFP land use raster into four classes (forest, agricultural, anthropogenic, aquatic), calculates area (m²) of each land use class per sub-watershed via zonal histogram and pixel-area scaling (100 m² per 10×10 m pixel), optionally aggregates dam drainage areas (from CEHQ dam points) per sub-watershed using D8-based basin delineation and spatial join summation, and outputs a vector layer of sub-watershed polygons with attributes: segment ID, total watershed area, forest_area, agri_area, anthro_area, water_area, land_area, and dam_area_sum.

The script burns vector-based drainage networks into a digital elevation model (DEM) by rasterizing the drainage layers, converting both DEM and drainage to PCRaster format, preparing a boolean drainage mask using cover, and applying a custom 'burndem' algorithm that creates a smooth drop over a user-defined buffer distance and an additional sharp drop directly at the drainage line. The output is a modified DEM raster where elevation values are lowered along and near drainage features to enforce hydrological connectivity.

task_name: Derive watershed basin from DEM and discharge point
task_description: The script computes the upslope drainage basin for a user-specified discharge point using a filled DEM and SAGA GIS 'upslopearea' algorithm. It then converts the resulting raster basin to vector (polygonized), fixes geometries, dissolves features, filters to retain only the target watershed, clips the DEM to that basin, generates contour lines at 100 m intervals, clips the input channel network to the basin boundary, and computes watershed-level statistics and Curve Numbers (CN) by intersecting with soil and Corine land cover layers. Outputs include: (1) raw and filtered basin polygons (GPKG), (2) clipped basin DEM (GeoTIFF), (3) 100-m contour lines (GPKG), (4) basin-restricted channel network (GPKG), (5) CN-weighted polygon layer (GPKG), and (6) Corine and SCS land use classification layers (GPKG).

The script computes a kernel density estimation (KDE) heatmap from an input point vector layer using QGIS's native 'qgis:heatmapkerneldensityestimation' algorithm, then applies a pseudocolor raster style (including color ramp selection, inversion, interpolation mode, classification mode, and number of gradient classes) via the custom 'densityanalysis:rasterstyle' algorithm. Outputs include a styled raster density map with user-configurable pixel size, kernel radius (converted to CRS units), kernel shape, decay (for triangular), output scaling, and styling parameters. All parameters are exposed as QGIS Processing inputs with validation and feedback reporting.

The script extracts outlet points from a segmented stream network by interpolating points near the downstream ends of each line segment (using a dynamic distance based on segment length), rasterizes the stream network using a LiDAR-derived 10 m DEM, snaps the interpolated points to the nearest stream pixel within 40 m using WhiteboxTools' JensonSnapPourPoints, and joins the original segment ID attribute (e.g., 'Id_UEA') from the stream network to the snapped points via nearest-neighbor join (max distance 50 m). The output is a point vector layer where each feature represents a snapped outlet with its associated segment identifier.

task_name: Convert GWSW sewer network to GeoDyn input
task_description: The script converts a municipal sewer network dataset (GWSW) into GeoDyn-compatible input layers for hydrodynamic modeling. It processes vector layers representing bemalingsgebieden (catchments), netwerk_knooppunt (nodes), netwerk_kunstwerk (structures like pumps, overflows, and culverts), and netwerk_verbinding (pipes). Key steps include: (1) extracting and filtering structures by type (e.g., 'Pomp', 'Doorlaatniveau', 'Overstortdrempel'); (2) spatially joining pipes to catchments using 'within' and 'nearest' relationships; (3) generating BEM_ID and STELSEL_ID identifiers; (4) computing storage volumes in pipes ('Berging_leiding_parts') and nodes ('BergingInKnopen') based on geometry, pipe/structure dimensions, and elevation data (e.g., 'Maaiveldhoogte', 'Drempelniveau', 'BobBeginpuntLeiding'); (5) aggregating per-catchment statistics (counts of pumps, overflows, culverts; total storage in m³); and (6) producing standardized output layers including 'Gebiedsgegevens_punt_tbv_stap2' (point features with attributes like BERGING_M3, POMPEN_ST, OVERSTORT_, DOORLAAT_S) and 'Gebiedsgegevens_lijn_tbv_stap2' (line features joined with storage values). All outputs are structured for direct ingestion into the GeoDyn modeling suite.

The script performs spatial interpolation of a user-specified numeric field (e.g., soil nutrient concentration, pH, or moisture) from point vector data to generate a continuous raster surface. It supports four methods: Thiessen (nearest-neighbor tessellation), Voronoi (geometric partitioning), Delaunay triangulation (with attribute joining), and Inverse Distance Weighting (IDW) via GRASS v.surf.idw. For tessellation methods, it first creates polygons (Thiessen/Voronoi/Delaunay), clips them to the convex hull of input points, then rasterizes the resulting vector layer using the specified field and pixel resolution. For IDW, it directly invokes GRASS IDW interpolation. Outputs are a single GeoTIFF raster at user-defined grid resolution (meters).

The script performs spatial sampling of a user-provided raster layer by generating point features at pixel centers and selecting a user-defined number of points either randomly (unstratified) or stratified by reclassifying the raster into quantiles, equal intervals, or K-means classes. For stratified sampling, it first applies a custom classification algorithm ('Precision Agriculture:R - Classification'), converts the classified raster to points, filters out 'nan' values, then performs random selection within each class subset. The final output is a vector layer of sampling points with added X/Y coordinate fields.

The script computes the Revised Universal Soil Loss Equation (RUSLE) erosion potential raster using a filled-sinks DEM and optional or single-value K, C, and R factor inputs. It first calculates the LS factor using the 'LS Mitasova' algorithm (which derives slope, flow accumulation, and LS from the DEM with user-defined sheet and rill erosion factors), then constructs a dynamic raster algebra expression (e.g., 'A*B*C*D' or substituted numeric values) combining LS, K, C, and R components via GDAL's raster calculator.
